rows.evidence: Q1: Methods 2.1-2.4 and Results 3.1-3.6 <U+2013> the authors run their own multivariate empirical (MVE) stochastic simulations of cotton yield and price, validated against a four-year Bushland field experiment (Table 1, Table 2), and conduct their own enterprise-budget and SERF risk analysis of net returns for MESA, LESA, LEPA and SDI at 25-100% ET replacement.
rows.notes: The study contains nothing about electricity/power connections, metering, or pump energy pricing as a condition for groundwater savings, and it does not measure groundwater extraction under adoption. What it actually shows is an economic result: SDI produced similar net return at 75% and 100% ET replacement (Sections 3.4, 4; Fig. 5, Fig. 9), from which the authors infer that irrigation water could be saved with SDI at the 75% ET level without loss of profit, and that policies/financial incentives would be needed to motivate water saving under spray and LEPA systems. The claim that reduction in groundwater extraction occurs 'only when the power connection is metered' is not supported by any result in this paper; the water-use figures (Fig. 2) are applied irrigation amounts from the experiment, essentially equal across systems at each ET level, not an adoption-driven extraction reduction. Yield data derive from Colaizzi et al. (2004, 2005, 2010), but co-authors overlap and the simulation/economic analysis is the authors' own, so Q1 is yes.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary tables/figures (Table S1, Figs. S1-S5) not included but not needed for the rating.
